docs.title: Crosswork CNC Hands-on
docs.text:
This is the operator lab for Cisco Crosswork Network Controller (CNC) 7.2.0. You will use the dCloud session from chapter 1: one CNC, a five-node IOS-XR lab, and a dedicated SR-PCE lab.

Each chapter has an objective, the clicks or CLI, the result you should see, and a short Done when list. Router work in this lab is show output unless a chapter says otherwise. Configuration changes go through CNC.

docs.title: Lab story
docs.text:
1. Bring CNC out of maintenance and start both CML labs.
  2. Confirm CNC, the providers, and collection are healthy.
  3. Read the topology in the UI and confirm it from XR CLI.
  4. Walk inventory, faults, configuration, and performance.
  5. Create PCC-initiated SRv6 policies with PCE-delegated dynamic paths. (Optional)
  6. Provision an L3VPN.
  7. Provision a L2VPN VPWS and check its Service Health.
  8. Provision a L2VPN VPLS with multi-homing and check its Service Health.
  9. Collect showtech, read collection jobs and alarms, and walk the patch screen.

docs.title: 1. Preparation
docs.text:
Time: 10 minutes

Objective: Access the dCloud environment, disable maintenance mode, start the CML labs, and log in to a controller that is ready for use.

Instructor

Maintenance mode shuts down the applications gracefully, and bringing them back takes several minutes.

docs.title: 1.1 Lab setup and CNC
docs.text:
The lab setup In this scenario, the lab setup is as follows.

  • CNC version 7.2.0 Single VM
  • P and PE routers: Cisco 8711-32FH-M (VXR) on CML (25.4.2)
  • PCE: XRv9k on CML (25.4.1)
  • CE routers: CSR 1000v on CML (17.03.08a)

The P and PE routers use the Cisco 8000 hardware emulator on CML. For more information about the Cisco 8000 hardware emulator, refer to the following:

https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/iosxr/cisco8000-emulator/cisco8000-hardware-emulator-installation-guide.pdf.

XRv9k for the PCE and CSR1000V for the CEs run in a different CML instance, which is connected to the first one by multiple external connectors.

The difference between Single VM (SVM) and cluster There are two types of CNC deployment: Single VM (SVM) and cluster. In Single VM deployment, all nodes, NSO, and Crosswork Data Gateway (CDG) run in a single VM. In cluster deployment, each component is set up as a separate VM.

docs.title: 1.2 Disable maintenance mode
docs.text:
Use maintenance mode to temporarily suspend Crosswork Network Controller operations for maintenance or restart activities, and then resume normal service. Maintenance mode gracefully shuts down the system for updates and synchronizes application data before it suspends services.

For more information about maintenance mode, refer to the following:

https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/cloud-systems-management/crosswork-infrastructure/7-2/AdminGuide/b-cisco-crosswork-admin-guide-7-2/g-vm-management/t-manage-maintenance-mode-settings.html

Follow the steps below to confirm that maintenance mode is off. If it is on, disable it.

  1. Sign in to dCloud and click the "View" button (note that the scenario name may be different).
  2. Access Ubuntu2204-1T-Desktop (use VM Console) and run Firefox on the desktop. Click the "CNC" bookmark to access CNC (https://[2001:db8:134::200]:30603). After you log in, the dashboard is displayed.
  3. Go to Administration > Settings > System Settings > Maintenance Mode.
  4. If a popup already offers to turn maintenance mode off, accept it.

  5. If the Maintenance slider is On, drag it to Off.

  6. Wait for about 20 to 30 minutes for the applications to restart.

Result: The maintenance slider stays Off, and the UI loads the normal home page.

docs.title: 1.3 Confirm CML labs are running
docs.text:
In this lab, two CML instances are connected through multiple external connectors. Review the network topology and familiarize yourself with the connections.

Follow the steps below to confirm that both CML instances are up and running.

  1. Open another tab in Firefox and click the "CML2 for XR" bookmark.
  2. Confirm that the "5-nodes_L3VPN 8711-32FH 25.4.2-ipv6" scenario is running. If not, start the scenario.
  3. Open another tab in Firefox and click the "CML2 for PCE" bookmark.
  4. Confirm that the "xrv9k-25.4.1-pce-for-CNC7.2-ipv6" scenario is running. If not, start the scenario.

Result: The labs are booted. CNC can reach the devices once the providers and the Data Gateway are healthy. You confirm that reachability in the next chapter.

docs.title: 1.4 Sync-from devices
docs.text:
A key component of CNC is Network Services Orchestrator (NSO). NSO stores device configurations in an internal database called CDB. The device configuration and the CDB must be in sync for CNC to provision services.

If there is a difference, the state changes to "out-of-sync". In that case, run "sync-from" in Device Management to synchronize the configuration between NSO and the devices.

Follow the steps below to get familiar with the sync operation.

  1. Access CNC and go to Device Management > Network Devices.
  2. Select all devices and choose Sync-from devices to NSO from Actions.
  3. Go to Inventory Jobs and wait for the job to complete.
  4. Open NSO by clicking the "NSO" button in the top right.
  5. Click "SSO Login" to log in to NSO. You do not need to enter a username or password.

Result: All devices are synced with CNC. You are logged in to the UI, and the controller is in normal operating mode.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You are logged in to CNC.
  • Maintenance mode is Off.
  • The CML labs are booted.
  • All devices are synced.

docs.title: 2. CNC management
docs.text:
Time: 15 minutes.

Objective: Confirm that CNC 7.2 is healthy enough for topology, inventory, traffic engineering, and service provisioning. You are reading the system, not rebuilding it.

The rest of the lab depends on three things:

Later work Depends on Topology and SR policies SR-PCE provider, BGP-LS and PCEP from the routers Inventory, alarms, interface counters Data Gateway collection jobs L3VPN and L2VPN provisioning NSO provider, devices in sync

docs.title: 2.1 Crosswork Summary and Crosswork Health
docs.text:
You can verify the health of CNC in Crosswork Manager. In this section, review the Crosswork status and packages.

  1. From the main menu, go to Administration > Crosswork Manager.
  2. Stay on the Crosswork Summary tab. Read the tiles for the cluster (or single VM), Platform Infrastructure, and the installed applications.
  3. Open System summary. Confirm the VM is up and that CPU, memory, and disk are not in a warning state.
  4. Open the Crosswork Health tab.
  5. For each of the following applications, open the tile and confirm that the application (and its microservices) is Healthy or Running:
    • Platform Infrastructure
    • Optimization Engine
    • Service Health, if it is installed (chapters 7 and 8 use it)
    • Element Management Functions
    • Active Topology
  6. Open Alarms or Events on an application tile only to check whether any alarm is raised against the platform itself. Device alarms are covered in chapter 4 and chapter 9.

Result: You can name the applications this lab uses and their health states.

docs.title: 2.2 Providers
docs.text:
Crosswork Network Controller components depend on external services, such as Cisco Crosswork Network Services Orchestrator (NSO) and Segment Routing Path Computation Element (SR-PCE), to perform operations like configuration modifications and segment routing path calculations. To manage access and facilitate information sharing among Crosswork Network Controller components, each external service must have a configured provider that belongs to a specific provider family (for example, NSO or SR-PCE).

For more information, refer to the following.

https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/cloud-systems-management/crosswork-infrastructure/7-2/AdminGuide/b-cisco-crosswork-admin-guide-7-2/g-DLM/c-providers.html

Follow the steps below to confirm the providers.

  1. Go to Administration > Manage Provider Access.
  2. Find the SR-PCE provider that points at the PCE CML lab (xrv9k-25.4.1-pce-for-CNC7.2-ipv6). Check its reachability and protocol state. The provider should be reachable, with the topology feed up.
  3. Find the NSO provider. You can also open NSO from the top-right menu.
  4. Open a provider only to see its credential profile name. The profile is a reference; the password stays in the profile store.

Result: SR-PCE and NSO are both reachable.

If SR-PCE is down, do not proceed to chapter 3. If NSO is down, you can still go through topology and element management, but wait until NSO is reachable before starting chapters 6 and 7.

docs.title: 2.3 Data Gateway and collection at a glance
docs.text:
Interface counters, inventory detail, syslog, and SNMP traps arrive through a Crosswork Data Gateway (CDG). This dCloud session may use a dedicated Data Gateway VM or the embedded collector on a single VM. Either way, devices must be attached and collection must be running.

  1. Go to Administration > Data Gateway Management. (cluster only)
  2. Confirm the gateway (or pool) is enrolled and administratively Up. (cluster only)
  3. Open the gateway and confirm the XR lab devices are attached to it. (cluster only)
  4. Open Administration > Collection Jobs (or Administration > Data Gateway Management > Collection Jobs, depending on the build).
  5. On Bulk jobs, confirm that system jobs are in the READY or Successful state, not Failed.

Result: You can identify the collector that feeds inventory, alarms, and utilization. You will read collection jobs in more detail in chapter 9.

docs.title: 2.4 What you should not change
docs.text:
Credential profiles, AAA, certificates, backup jobs, and licensing are visible from Administration and from Device Management > Credential Profiles. Open a profile only if a device is unreachable and you need to check the profile name.

Backup, restore, and Add OS patch put the cluster into maintenance mode. Patching is a guided walkthrough in chapter 9. Do not start it here.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Platform Infrastructure, Optimization Engine, Active Topology, and Element Management Functions are Healthy or Running.
  • The SR-PCE provider is reachable.
  • The NSO provider is reachable.
  • A Data Gateway (or embedded collector) is Up and the XR devices are attached.
  • Collection jobs are not in a Failed state.

docs.title: 3. Active Topology
docs.text:
Time: 15 minutes.

Objective: Use Crosswork Active Topology to identify where a device is located and how it is connected, then verify the same facts from the IOS-XR CLI.

Active Topology is the map. Optimization Engine draws traffic-engineering objects on top of the same topology. You will use both views, then open a PE console from CML.

This lab uses IPv6. The IS-IS, BGP-LS, SRv6 locator, and PCEP information on the routers should match what the map shows.

docs.title: 3.1 Open the map
docs.text:
There are many ways for CNC to onboard devices. In this lab, devices are onboarded via PCE (Path Computation Element). The benefit of onboarding devices via PCE is that the topology is also automatically discovered by using link-state information.

For more information about onboarding devices, please refer to following:

https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/cloud-systems-management/crosswork-infrastructure/7-2/AdminGuide/b-cisco-crosswork-admin-guide-7-2/g-add-and-configure-devices/c-device-onboarding-methods.html

Follow the steps below to confirm the onboarded devices and topology.

  1. From the main menu, open Topology.
  2. Wait for the devices from 5-nodes_L3VPN 8711-32FH 25.4.2-ipv6 to appear. An empty map usually means that the SR-PCE provider is up but BGP-LS is still down, or that the CML nodes are still booting. Recheck chapter 2.
  3. Routers are placed on the geographic map based on the longitude and latitude configured in Device Management.
  4. Identify the three provider-edge (PE) routers. They serve as the headend and the endpoints in chapters 5 through 8.
  5. Each line color indicates the utilization of the link. The threshold for the color can be customized by going to Administration > Settings > Topology > Metric thresholds. Try 0.0000001 (six zeros after the dot) and see if the link color changes.

Result: You can find all three PEs and at least one IGP path between them.

docs.title: 3.2 Read a device and a link in CNC
docs.text:
1. Select the headend. Open the Device details panel.
  2. Record hostname, management IPv6 address, reachability, and IGP router ID.
  3. Select a core link on a path between any two routers.
  4. In the link details, record:
    • Interface names on each side
    • IGP metric
    • TE metric
    • Utilization
  5. Switch the layer to Traffic Engineering and confirm SRv6 locators.

docs.title: 3.3 Confirm the same topology from XR CLI
docs.text: Open a new tab in Firefox and click the "CML2 for XR" bookmark to access the XR routers. Open a console on the headend PE. Stay in EXEC mode. Do not enter configuration mode.

docs.title: Neighbors and IGP
docs.text:
show isis neighbors
show isis ipv6 topology

If the lab uses a named IS-IS instance, the instructor will give you the instance name. In that case, use:

show isis instance <name> neighbors
show isis instance <name> ipv6 topology

Match each IS-IS neighbor to a node on the CNC map. The neighbor count and the path you traced in section 3.2 should agree.

docs.title: Addressing
docs.text:
show ipv6 interface brief
show interface <core-interface> brief

Confirm that the core interface you clicked on the map is up/up and that its IPv6 address matches the link details in CNC.

docs.title: SRv6
docs.text:
show segment-routing srv6 locator
show segment-routing srv6 sid

The locator prefix on the PE should match the SRv6 layer on the map. If the map shows a locator and the CLI does not, the topology feed is stale. Wait and refresh; do not configure a locator.

docs.title: How CNC learned this topology
docs.text:
On the PE:

show bgp link-state link-state
show bgp link-state link-state summary

On the SR-PCE (in the second CML lab), if the instructor gives you access to that console:

show pce ipv6 peer
show pce ipv6 topology summary

The PCE should list the PEs as BGP-LS and PCEP peers. That is the feed behind the CNC map.

Result: Hostname, neighbor, core interface, and SRv6 locator agree between CNC and CLI.

docs.title: 3.4 Dashboard baseline
docs.text:
1. Return to the home page or the topology dashboard.
  2. Record the reachable-device count and the SR policy count.
  3. Zero SR policies is acceptable before chapter 5. You will compare the policy count after you create the SR policies in chapter 5.

Result: You have a baseline count of devices and policies.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• All three lab PEs are on the map and reachable.
  • show isis neighbors (or the named-instance form) matches the map.
  • The core interface and SRv6 locator you recorded in CNC appear in XR CLI.
  • You know the baseline SR policy count.

docs.title: 4. Element management
docs.text:
Time: 20 minutes.

Objective: Use CNC Element Management Functions to check node status, hardware inventory, configuration archive, alarms, and interface performance. Do not change any device configuration in this chapter.

Element Management Functions in CNC 7.2 cover device onboarding, inventory, faults, metrics, software images, configuration backup, and configuration templates.

docs.title: Compare CNC with a generic NMS (Network Management System)
docs.text:
CNC is the controller view of the same devices, with IGP and SR context. The following table compares CNC with a generic NMS.

Generic NMS CNC What is different Node list, ICMP/SNMP reachability Device Management > Network Devices CNC also shows the credential profile and the Data Gateway mapping that collection uses Hardware inventory (chassis, modules, serials) Device Management > Network Inventory Same concept: serial number, product ID, and alarm badge on each part Network map Topology (chapter 3) The CNC map is built from IGP/SRv6 information from SR-PCE, not only from Layer 3 discovery Alert console / trap viewer Alerts > Alarms and Events CNC splits system, network, and device alarms. An alarm stays until it clears; an event is a point in time Interface utilization and thresholds Device Management > Performance Policies, plus link utilization on the topology map CNC Optimization Engine colors links from collected counters. Performance Policies raise threshold-crossing alarms NCM config archive, compare, restore Device Management > Configuration Backup and Restore CNC can also back up on configuration change. Restore is out of scope for this lab NCM config change jobs / scripts Device Management > Configuration Templates Parameterized CLI (Apache Velocity). These are different from the NSO L2/L3VPN templates in chapters 6 and 7

Use the table to map generic NMS functions to CNC. The rest of this chapter covers the CNC side.

docs.title: 4.1 Detailed inventory
docs.text:
1. In Topology, click any node, for example C8711-4-P, then click Detailed inventory button.
  2. You will see the hierarchical view of the inventory. Explore the graph and see how easy it is to grasp the relationship between the inventory.

docs.title: 4.2 Network devices and inventory
docs.text:
1. Go to Device Management > Network Devices.
  2. Find the headend from chapter 3. Record operational state, reachability, and the credential profile name.
  3. Go to Device Management > Network Inventory.
  4. Filter by the headend hostname (C8711-1-PE) or product family.
  5. Open the chassis, one route processor or line card, and one pluggable if the inventory lists them.
  6. Read the alarm summary on that inventory row.

Result: You can navigate from a hostname to a chassis and a module.

If a device stays unreachable, check its credentials, IPv6 reachability to the management address, and whether the CML node has booted.

docs.title: 4.3 Configuration backup
docs.text:
CNC archives device configurations, compares two archives, and can restore them. In this lab, you only view the archive, as in an NCM config view.

  1. Go to Device Management > Configuration Backup and Restore.
  2. Find the headend.
  3. Open the latest archived configuration. Identify the hostname and the segment-routing or IS-IS section.
  4. If two archives exist, open the comparison and note one difference, or confirm that they match.
  5. Do not use Schedule backup or Restore.

Result: You have viewed an actual archived configuration for the headend.

When automatic backup on configuration change is enabled under Device Management > Configuration Preferences, the archive stays useful after chapters 6 and 7. Check the preference and leave the values unchanged.

docs.title: 4.4 Configuration templates (read only)
docs.text:
Device templates under Device Management are parameterized CLI scripts. They are intended for repeatable underlay or day-1 configuration. They are not the NSO L2VPN/L3VPN function-pack templates.

  1. Go to Device Management > Configuration Templates.
  2. Open one existing template, if any exist. Read the device types it targets and one variable it expects.
  3. You can use configuration templates to run a set of commands. Create a new template with the following values:
    • Name: collect-outputs
    • Enable "Read template for troubleshooting"
    • Authorization: admin
  4. Select "Cisco 8711-32FH" as the device type.
  5. Do not define any variables. Click Next.
  6. Enter the show commands in Configure template script.
  7. Deploy the template you created.
  8. Go to Jobs to check the progress.

docs.title: 4.5 Alarms and events
docs.text:
1. Go to Alerts > Alarms and Events.
  2. Stay on Alarms. Use the category list to see system, network, and device alarms as separate sets.
  3. Filter to the headend if the filter allows it.
  4. If an alarm is present, record severity, source, and whether it is acknowledged. Do not acknowledge, clear, or annotate alarms unless the instructor assigns a lab alarm to you.
  5. Switch Show from Alarms to Events.
  6. Read the newest event. An event is a moment in time. An alarm remains until it clears.

Result: You can open both views. An empty alarm list is normal on a healthy CML lab.

You will use this page again in chapter 9.

docs.title: 4.6 Performance
docs.text:
Link colors on the topology map come from interface utilization collected for Optimization Engine. Element Management Functions add polling policies.

  1. Go to Device Management > Performance Policies.
  2. Click Create new policy and see what other policies can be created.
  3. Open one existing policy, if any exist. Read which devices it covers, how often it polls, and which threshold raises an alarm.
  4. Return to the Topology and click any link. Open History and confirm the utilization and traffic rate.
  5. Leave the policy enable/disable switch unchanged.

Result: You know where a threshold is defined, and you can identify one live counter.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You can map the generic NMS functions (node list, inventory, alerts, config archive, and utilization) to the corresponding CNC pages.
  • The headend is in Network Devices and in Network Inventory.
  • You opened an archived configuration and did not restore it.
  • You opened Alarms and Events.
  • You compared one interface counter with the topology utilization from chapter 3.

docs.title: 5. SR-TE and SRv6 (Optional)
docs.text:
Time: 60 minutes.

Objective: Create various PCC-initiated SRv6 policies with PCE-delegated dynamic paths from CNC.

Note

At the time of writing, Cisco 8000 platforms are yet to support SRv6 policies with head-end computed dynamic paths or PCE-initiated SRv6 policies. In addition, the CNC 7.2 built-in function pack does not support explicit paths that use IPv6 addresses or SRv6 SIDs. Therefore, this hands-on focuses on PCC-initiated SRv6 policies with PCE-delegated dynamic paths. For details, see Cisco 8000 Configuration Guide: Segment Routing over IPv6 Traffic Engineering (SRv6-TE)

docs.title: 5.1 Terminology
docs.text: Term Meaning in this lab PCC The headend router. It holds the policy configuration and has a PCEP session with SR-PCE. PCE SR-PCE in the second CML lab. It learns the topology through BGP-LS, computes paths, and reports the policies to CNC. PCC-initiated The policy configuration resides on the headend. In this lab, you create it in CNC, and CNC provisions the configuration on the headend through NSO. This is the type used in this chapter. PCE-delegated dynamic path A PCC-initiated candidate path with dynamic + pce. The headend delegates path computation to SR-PCE, and SR-PCE returns the SID list through PCEP. PCE-initiated The policy is created on SR-PCE and pushed to the headend through PCEP, without any configuration on the headend. Not used in this lab because Cisco 8000 does not support it for SRv6. Color A number that identifies the intent. Together with the endpoint, it identifies the policy. Chapter 6 binds an L3VPN to this color. Candidate path One way to reach the endpoint. The preference value determines which candidate path is selected.

docs.title: 5.2 Confirming the initial state
docs.text:
SR-PCE requires topology and SRv6 locator/SID information to compute paths. It acquires this information from the routers in the SRv6 topology via BGP-LS. In this scenario, BGP-LS sessions are established with the three PEs.

Open Firefox in private browsing mode and click the "CML2 for PCE" bookmark.

Then, on the SR-PCE console (cisco/cisco):


RP/0/RP0/CPU0:pce#show bgp link-state link-state neighbors brief
Wed Nov  4 06:02:58.271 UTC

Neighbor         Spk    AS  Description                         Up/Down  NBRState

2001:db8:1::52    0 65000                                         4d20h Established  
2001:db8:1::53    0 65000                                         4d20h Established  
RP/0/RP0/CPU0:pce#

PCEP (Path Computation Element Communication Protocol) is a signaling protocol for exchanging SRv6-TE path information between an SR-PCE, which performs path computation, and the head-end routers (PCCs) in the network (RFC 5440).

PCEP handles bidirectional communication between routers and PCEs, including path computation requests (Request), reporting and updating of computed paths (Report/Update), and delegation of control (Delegation).

Open Firefox in private browsing mode and click the "CML2 for XR" bookmark. On the PCC routers (PE1, PE2, PE3):

docs.title: 5.3 Create PCC-initiated policy 1 (Exclude RED link)
docs.text:
Configure an SRv6-TE policy with the following conditions:

  • Policy Name: PE1-PE2_color10
  • Headend: PE1
  • Endpoint: PE2
  • Optimization: IGP
  • Constraint: exclude RED link

Since all links in this topology use the default cost, the path from PE1 to PE2 is computed as follows, avoiding the link between P4 and PE2.

You can configure the policy using either of the following two methods. Option 1: Manually configure parameters Option 2: Import JSON

docs.title: Option 5-3-1: Manually configure parameters
docs.text:
1. Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > Traffic Engineering, SRv6 tab, then click Create > PCC-init.

  2. Click the + button.

  3. Set the following:

    • name: PE1-PE2_color10
    • headend: C8711-1-PE
    • tail-end: 2001:db8::2
    • color: 10
    • preference: 100
    • st-te-path-choice: dynamic-path (enable dynamic and select pce)
    • metric-type: igp
    • constraints: enable affinity and add a rule with an action exclude-any color RED.
    • srv6: enable locator (locator-name: srv6, behavior: ub6-insert-reduced, and binding-sid-type: srv6-dynamic).

  4. Click Dry-run to confirm the configuration.

    You can switch the display by using Show changes in the upper right.

  5. Click Commit changes.

docs.title: Option 5-3-2: Import JSON
docs.text:
You can also configure the policy by loading a JSON file. The sample JSON files were exported from the following screen.

In this lab, load the JSON file prepared in advance by using the procedure below.

  1. Open a terminal and clone the JSON file repository from Git.

    git clone https://github.com/mekawaba/cnc-payloads.git

  2. Load Home > cnc-payloads > PE1-PE2_color10.json.

    "cisco-sr-te-cfp:sr-te": {

        "policy": [
          {
            "name": "PE1-PE2_color10",
            "head-end": [
              {
                "name": "C8711-1-PE"
              }
            ],
            "srv6": {
              "locator": {
                "locator-name": "srv6",
                "behavior": "ub6-insert-reduced",
                "binding-sid-type": "srv6-dynamic"
              }
            },
            "tail-end": "2001:db8::2",
            "color": 10,
            "path": [
              {
                "preference": 100,
                "dynamic": {
                  "constraints": {
                    "affinity": {

                          "color": [
                            "RED"
                          ]

                      ]
                    }
                  },
                  "pce": {},
                  "metric-type": "igp"
                }
              }
            ]
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  }

  3. Confirm that the following parameters are set.

    • name: PE1-PE2_color10
    • headend: C8711-1-PE
    • endpoint: 2001:db8::2
    • color: 10
    • preference: 100
    • st-te-path-choice: dynamic-path (enable dynamic and select pce)
    • metric-type: igp
    • constraints: enable affinity and add a rule with an action exclude-any color RED.
    • srv6: enable locator (locator-name: srv6, behavior: ub6-insert-reduced, and binding-sid-type: srv6-dynamic).

  4. Click Dry-run to confirm the configuration.

    You can switch the display by using Show changes in the upper right.

  5. Click Commit changes.

docs.title: 6. L3VPN provisioning
docs.text:
Time: 30 minutes.

Objective: Create one L3VPN from CNC. NSO renders the device configuration from the IETF L3VPN network model.

docs.title: 6.1 What you are about to commit
docs.text: Field Value Service name CustA Endpoints PE1, PE2, PE3 Route distinguisher and route targets 100:100 Transport SRv6

docs.title: 6.2 Pre-check
docs.text:
MP-BGP configuration is not supported by the built-in function pack in CNC 7.2. Because of CML licensing constraints (limited to 5 devices), a route reflector (RR) is not used in this topology. Therefore, verify that MP-BGP is configured in a full mesh between the PEs.

docs.title: 7. L2VPN VPWS provisioning
docs.text:
Time: 30 minutes

Objective: Provision a point-to-point L2VPN (VPWS) from CNC.

CNC 7.2 provisions services based on the IETF L2VPN network model through NSO. VPWS is a point-to-point wire between two attachment circuits.

Field Value Service name CustB_vpws vpn-type point-to-point (vpws-evpn) Endpoints PE1, PE2 Transport SRv6

docs.title: 7.1 Pre-check (ID-Pools)
docs.text:
EVI IDs and Source/Target IDs can be automatically assigned from predefined pools. It is also possible to set fixed values.

In this lab, confirm that those pools are already configured.

  1. Resource pools (ranges of assignable values) are located under Service & Traffic Engineering > Provisioning (NSO) > Global > Resource Pool.

    • evi-id-pool: Pool for EVI IDs
    • evi-source-target-pool: Pool for Source/Target IDs

    By clicking Edit under Actions, you can see that the following values are set for each pool. After confirming the values, close the dialog with Cancel.

    • evi-id-pool: 100-500

    • evi-source-target-pool: 1-100

  2. Confirm that these pools are referenced in the L2VPN configuration under L2VPN > ID-Pools.

    • evi-id-pool-name: evi-id-pool
    • evi-source-target-pool-name: evi-source-target-pool

docs.title: 8.6 Packet Capture (Optional)
docs.text:
Use the packet capture feature of CML to observe the encapsulation in the IPv6 header.

Unicast Traffic (uDT2U) 1. Start a ping from CE1 to CE2. Due to lab constraints, the ping may not succeed, but this is not a problem.

On CE1(csr1000v-CE1):
ce1#ping 198.21.0.200 repeat 10

  1. Right-click the link between P5 and PE3 and start a packet capture.

  2. Select the ICMP echo request packet from 198.21.0.100 to 198.21.0.200.

  3. Find the IPv6 header. The destination address contains the uDT2U SID of PE3 (for example, fcbb:bb00:3:e002::).

docs.title: 9. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Time: 30 minutes.

Objective: Collect CNC showtech, read collection jobs, read alarms, and review the add-patch workflow. Whether to apply a patch is the instructor's decision, because CNC enters maintenance mode to install it.

This chapter covers troubleshooting the controller, not changing router configuration.

docs.title: 9.1 Alarms
docs.text:
1. Go to Alerts > Alarms and Events.
  2. Filter Alarms by category: system, network, and device.
  3. For each category, record whether any alarm is raised. System alarms relate to CNC itself (disk, application, collector). Device alarms relate to the XR nodes.
  4. Open one alarm if any exist. Record severity, source, time, and description. Do not acknowledge or clear alarms unless the instructor assigns that alarm to you.
  5. Switch to Events and find the event that triggered the alarm, if one exists.

Result: You know whether the platform, the network, or a device currently has a problem.

Use alarms together with the health tiles from chapter 2. An application tile can show Healthy while a system alarm is active; the alarm provides the detail.

docs.title: 9.2 Collection jobs
docs.text:
Empty inventory, blank utilization, and Service Health stuck on Initiated are usually collection problems, not VPN problems.

  1. Go to Administration > Collection Jobs, or Administration > Data Gateway Management > Collection Jobs.
  2. Open Bulk jobs. Bulk jobs are created by the system, the UI, or the API. Record the Status (for example, Successful) and the Context ID.

  3. Open a successful job and read the device names.

  4. Review the details in Job Monitoring.

  5. If a job is Degraded, open the job details and read the error. Common causes:

    • Device not attached to a Data Gateway
    • Incorrect SNMP or CLI credentials
    • Device unreachable (the CLI checks in chapter 3 would already have shown this)
    • Destination in Error state (collection still runs, but the error count increases)

  6. Review the job distribution details to understand the difference between Collection and Distribution.

Result: You can locate the jobs and check their status.

docs.title: 9.3 Showtech
docs.text: Collect showtech before you open a TAC case. CNC 7.2 collects cluster logs and metrics from Crosswork Manager. Application showtech is collected per application. Data Gateway showtech is a separate encrypted download.

docs.title: Cluster and application
docs.text:
1. Go to Administration > Crosswork Manager.
  2. Open Crosswork Summary > System summary.
  3. Click Actions and note the showtech options:
    • Request all — logs and metrics
    • Request metrics
    • Request logs
  4. If the instructor wants a file from this VM, collect logs (not Request all) so that the bundle stays small. Otherwise, only open Actions > View showtech jobs and review any previous job.
  5. To collect showtech for one application, return to Crosswork Health, open the application tile (for example Service Health or Platform Infrastructure), and use that tile's showtech action. Application logs are collected separately from the cluster bundle.
  6. In View showtech jobs, check the status. Publish or download a file only if the instructor needs it. Do not delete anything.

Result: You know where to start cluster showtech and application showtech, and you did not fill the disk with a collection the instructor did not ask for.

docs.title: Data Gateway (cluster only)
docs.text:
1. Go to Administration > Data Gateway Management.
  2. Select the gateway.
  3. Open Actions and find Download Showtech.
  4. Do not download unless the instructor asks. The file is encrypted. The instructor holds the passphrase and decrypts the file if TAC requests it. Do not put a passphrase in chat or in this guide.

Result: You know where to find CDG showtech.

docs.title: 9.4 Add patch
docs.text: CNC 7.2 installs OS security patches (SPACK) from System management. Application bundles are added from Application Management. Both are maintenance operations. Adding an OS patch automatically turns maintenance mode on, applies the patch node by node, and then turns maintenance mode off. Rollback is not supported. Even on a small lab VM, the process takes a long time.

docs.title: OS patch screens
docs.text:
1. Go to Administration > Crosswork Manager.
  2. Open the System management tab.
  3. Find Add OS patch. Open the dialog only to check that the source can be a URL or SCP.
  4. Open System updates (or the list of already installed patches). Record whether this dCloud image already shows 7.2.0.
  5. Open Job History on the System management tab. Add-to-repository and per-VM apply jobs appear here after a patch is added. Review any existing job. Do not retry a job unless the instructor is recovering from a failed apply.
  6. After a successful apply (instructor only), verify the result in Administration > Crosswork Manager > System summary > Package details.

docs.title: Application file
docs.text:
1. Go to Administration > Crosswork Manager > Application Management.
  2. Note the Add new file option. It is used to upload an application CAPP file or a patch bundle.
  3. Do not upload a file unless the instructor provides one and asks you to.

docs.title: 9.5 If something from an earlier chapter is still broken
docs.text: Symptom First check Empty topology SR-PCE provider, BGP-LS, show pce ipv6 topology summary Device unreachable in Network Devices CML node booted, management IPv6, credential profile Thin inventory / no utilization Data Gateway attachment, collection job status SR policy preview empty SRv6 tab, show segment-routing srv6 locator, PCEP peer VPN out of sync NSO provider, Check sync, then chapter 7 optional sync-from only if asked Service Health stuck on Initiated Parameterized service-based collection job

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You opened Alarms and Events and recorded what is (or is not) raised.
  • You found bulk and parameterized collection jobs, including a service-based job for the VPWS when monitoring is on.
  • You can start cluster showtech from System summary and you know that application and CDG showtech are separate.
  • You reviewed Add OS patch and Job History without starting an unplanned maintenance window.

docs.title: 10. Optional: CNC MCP server
docs.text:
Time: 20 minutes

Objective: Ask the lab assistant one question that it can answer with a live Crosswork tool. Confirm the answer in the CNC UI.

The assistant is a chat page. When you ask a question, it may call tools on an MCP server. The MCP server communicates with CNC.

docs.title: 10.1 Open the assistant
docs.text:
Access Ubuntu2504-Desktop, open a terminal, and run the following: 

$ cd aiserver
$ ./main
Close the browser tab.

Access Ubuntu2204-1T-Desktop, open a terminal, and run the following: 

$ cd cnc_mcp
$ source venv/bin/activate
$ python3 cnc_mcp_server2.py

Open another terminal in Ubuntu2204-1T-Desktop and run the following: 

$ cd webui
$ source venv/bin/activate
$ streamlit run frontend.py

Result: The assistant is online and you can name the available tools.

docs.title: 10.2 One live question
docs.text:
In the chat, ask:

How many nodes are in the CNC?

Wait for the reply. Open the tool-call detail for that turn.

Confirm all of the following:

  • The assistant called the inventory count tool.
  • The reply contains a number.
  • You can find a matching count under Device Management > Network Devices or Network Inventory. The two screens group equipment differently, so the numbers may differ depending on what each one counts. Record both numbers and write one sentence explaining the difference. If they match, note that they match.

If the tool call fails, note the error text instead of relying on the model's guesses. A failure here usually means that the assistant cannot authenticate to CNC or cannot reach the UI address. In that case, ask the instructor to fix it. Chapters 2 and 4 already showed you the same inventory with your own login.

Result: You have a number from the tool and have compared it with Device Management.

docs.title: 10.3 Operator check (no write operations)
docs.text:
Ask a second question that does not require a write tool:

The inventory count is <the number you just verified>.
What should an operator check first in Crosswork?

A useful answer lists checks that you already know how to perform:

  • Reachability on Device Management > Network Devices
  • The credential profile on that device
  • Data Gateway mapping
  • Collection job status
  • SR-PCE and NSO provider status
  • Active alarms for that hostname

Pick one check the assistant suggested, open the corresponding CNC page, and verify whether the suggestion is correct. If the UI contradicts the assistant, trust the UI.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text: • The assistant answered the inventory question with a tool call, and you compared that number with Device Management.
